CH-F15E-CSAR-URANIUM.public_title: F-15E shootdown, missing airman, rescue, and uranium narrative
CH-F15E-CSAR-URANIUM.plain_english_summary: A real F-15E was lost and one airman was genuinely missing. The deceptive narrative was what Iranian official and state-media channels said happened next: the aircraft was first misidentified as an F-35; a capture story was promoted while Iranian authorities were still searching for the airman; rescue failure and Iranian-caused equipment losses were overstated; false remains evidence was presented; and, after both crew were recovered, the story shifted toward a nuclear/uranium mission explanation. Atlas keeps the real shootdown, the missing-airman period, the later F-15E correction, and real rescue-equipment losses as factual context rather than labeling those facts themselves as lies. The Apr. 9 signed analysis is attributed to Mohammad Molaei as author, while Press TV's separate act of publishing and amplifying it is assessed at the institutional level.
how_we_know: The underlying loss is real: a U.S. F-15E went down in Iran and one crew member remained missing while U.S. forces searched for him.
The original F-35 identification was wrong. Iranian reporting later corrected the aircraft type to F-15E using recovered wreckage and debris.

The capture branch is false, not merely unsupported. Tasnim reported that the missing airman was likely captured; a provincial IRGC unit later denied he had been captured or detained, Iranian authorities were still seeking his capture, and the airman was subsequently recovered by U.S. forces.
The early fact that the second airman had not yet been recovered was true. The categorical claim that the rescue ultimately failed was not: both crew members were recovered.

U.S. rescue aircraft and equipment were genuinely lost or damaged, but that does not establish Iran destroyed all of it. Independent reconstruction attributes part of the destroyed rescue package to U.S. denial action after aircraft became disabled.
Iranian official channels also presented supposed U.S. remains as evidence; the Iranian broadcasting system acknowledged the image was inaccurate or incorrect the next day.

Iran really did possess enriched uranium at Isfahan. That fact is not evidence that the observed rescue package was secretly a uranium-seizure mission. After the personnel-recovery outcome was established, later reporting substituted a nuclear/uranium mission narrative while preserving the same claimed Iranian victory.

The Lie finding comes from the combined chronology: repeated contradictions, corrections available inside the same state information system, direct institutional access to wreckage and battle-damage information, and later outcome-preserving narrative substitution. It is not based merely on the absence of proof or on a U.S. denial.

The Apr. 9 page was signed by Mohammad Molaei and carried as Press TV analysis. Atlas therefore does not impute Press TV's institutional knowledge to Molaei personally. His individual knowledge remains insufficiently established.

Press TV's publisher-level knowledge is separately assessable. Before publishing the Apr. 9 continuation, the outlet had already carried the rescue-specific record, its Apr. 6 F-15E correction, the Apr. 7 categorical nuclear-mission substitution, and reporting that stranded rescue equipment was destroyed by U.S. forces. Repetition after those correction opportunities materially weakens repeated innocent institutional error.

Several circulated images/videos tied to the pilot, rescue, and shootdown narrative are independently false or recycled. Atlas keeps those as separate media-artifact nodes because their official Iranian origin was not established; they support media-forensics conclusions, not automatic knowledge attribution to the IRGC or state officials.
CH-F15E-CSAR-URANIUM.event_title: F-15E shootdown, aircrew recovery, CSAR losses, and uranium narrative
CH-F15E-CSAR-URANIUM.event_baseline: A U.S. F-15E was lost over Iran. Both crew ejected; one was initially missing/evading. U.S. forces conducted a personnel-recovery operation, lost or damaged rescue equipment, and ultimately recovered both crew members.
CH-F15E-CSAR-URANIUM.terminal_event_state: The aircraft loss was real; the missing airman was not in established Iranian custody and both crew were recovered. Rescue-equipment losses were real but not all were caused by Iranian fire. Enriched uranium was associated with Isfahan, but that did not make the observed personnel-recovery mission a uranium-seizure raid.
open_evidence_gaps: The current record does not establish that the early hedged Tasnim capture report was knowingly false when first published.
Not every rescue-equipment loss has a fully public platform-by-platform causal reconstruction.
False third-party media tied to the pilot/rescue narrative is not attributed to an official Iranian origin absent authenticated provenance.
Mohammad Molaei's individual access to the counterfacts behind his Apr. 9 signed analysis is not established; this does not erase the separately supported Press TV institutional-knowledge inference.

CH-AIRCRAFT-KILL-AGGREGATES.public_title: Iranian U.S. aircraft and UAV cumulative kill-count narrative
CH-AIRCRAFT-KILL-AGGREGATES.plain_english_summary: Iran has reported a changing series of aircraft/UAV totals, but the denominator and metric do not stay constant: mixed drones, aircraft hit, aircraft targeted, and later type-specific MQ-9 ordinals are different propositions. Atlas therefore keeps each count and metric branch separate instead of treating the series as one cumulative confirmed-kill ledger.
how_we_know: The public series moves through 82, more than 130, 170, more than 170 aircraft hit including 16 fighters, and a 210 figure whose headline/body use different verbs.
Those figures are not interchangeable: drones downed, aircraft hit, aircraft targeted, and type-specific MQ-9 losses use different denominators and effects.

The Apr. 28 '16 fighters hit' proposition is distinct from the analytic question of whether that metric can be compared directly with earlier drone-down totals; the old model accidentally duplicated the same proposition ID for both.

The May 26 article itself provides the contradiction: the headline says about 210 were downed while the body reports language about being able to target around 210. The publication act is observable; the underlying '210 downed' assertion is the factual proposition.

Later 52nd/53rd MQ-9 ordinals require a type-specific reconciled ledger. Existing evidence supports substantial real MQ-9 attrition but does not establish those exact ordinals as either true or false.

CH-QATAR-PILOTS.public_title: Missing Iranian pilots and Qatar custody-access narrative

public_finding.label: False custody claim; likely lie on obstruction branch

CH-QATAR-PILOTS.plain_english_summary: Iranian aircraft and aircrew really were lost or went missing in the Qatar fighting. That factual baseline was incorrectly marked false in the old Ledger. The later claim that three missing pilots were alive in secret Qatari custody is a separate false proposition, and the subsequent claim that Qatar had simply kept an Iranian fact-finding team waiting for months is independently adjudicated as a likely lie.
how_we_know: The underlying Iranian aircraft/aircrew losses and missing-person problem are independently established; they are factual context, not the disputed custody claim.
Qatar denied secretly holding the pilots, reported recovery of one pilot's remains, and described an April invitation for Iran to review the search-and-rescue record.
The secret-custody allegation is therefore false on the completed record, while claimant knowledge remains less certain because Iran did not control Qatari detention systems.

The later obstruction claim is different. Qatar says it formally invited an Iranian team in April, Iran did not respond, and senior Iranian-Qatari diplomatic contact was already occurring. That makes the broad 'kept waiting for months' story materially harder to explain as simple lack of access.

Atlas does not let the false custody allegation contaminate the real aircraft-loss baseline, and does not let the stronger knowledge finding on the obstruction branch propagate backward to every earlier statement.

CH-INDIAN-OCEAN-DESTROYER.public_title: Indian Ocean U.S. destroyer/supply-ship strike narrative
CH-INDIAN-OCEAN-DESTROYER.plain_english_summary: The official claim that Iranian missiles hit a U.S. destroyer and refueling vessel remains unsubstantiated on the current physical/BDA record. Separately, video circulated as proof of the strike is definitely false: AFP traced it to a decommissioned U.S. ship sunk during RIMPAC 2022. The fake video does not by itself prove the official strike claim false, and its official Iranian origin has not been established.
how_we_know: The official strike/effect claim lacks independently identified corresponding U.S. warship damage in the reviewed record.
Remote maritime BDA can genuinely be uncertain, so absence of confirmed damage is not automatically a FALSE finding for the official claim.
The circulated proof video is a different proposition. AFP traced it to RIMPAC 2022 footage of a decommissioned U.S. ship.
Because official Iranian origin of that media artifact was not established, Atlas labels the artifact false without attributing a knowing fabrication to the official strike claimant.

CH-ALUDEID-BDA.plain_english_summary: Al Udeid suffered real, serious damage. The forensic question is the level of effect: radar/site damage and CAOC inoperability are supported, permanent destruction of the radar remains unresolved, and shorthand that the entire base was destroyed or unusable overstates the evidence. A separate viral 'before/after' satellite image used as proof of completely destroyed radar equipment is a false AI-manipulated media artifact; AFP traced it to a modified image of a U.S. base in Bahrain. The fake image does not erase the real Al Udeid damage and is not attributed to the IRGC or Iranian government without provenance.
how_we_know: Independent satellite imagery and later reporting confirm material strike damage at Al Udeid.
The AN/FPS-132 site was physically hit and materially degraded; available public evidence does not settle permanent repairability.
Separate reporting supports that the Combined Air Operations Center was rendered inoperable.
Those subfacility effects do not establish that the entire air base ceased operating.
The separate social-media shorthand record concerns the same physical event and therefore belongs inside this chain, not as another top-level event card.

AFP/Arab News found the viral radar image was AI-manipulated from a prior Google Earth image of a U.S. base in Bahrain. The image is false evidence even though real Al Udeid damage is independently established.

The source identifies Tehran Times as an amplifier of the image but does not establish that the IRGC or an Iranian government office created it; Atlas therefore withholds official-origin knowledge attribution.

CHAIN-CL-IRGC-ASSET-LIST.plain_english_summary: The IRGC published a detailed 15-day scorecard. The direct IRNA source now lets Atlas preserve the actual count/effect language and split the material claims instead of treating the whole list as one PARTLY_TRUE blob. Independent reporting proves the wider war caused real U.S. aircraft, air-defense, communications and base damage, but the current canonical record does not reconcile the scorecard's specific July 8–22 class-by-class counts. Each exact line item is therefore adjudicated separately and remains unresolved unless independent BDA supports that count and effect. The parent scorecard itself receives no Lie finding.
how_we_know: IRNA is now canonical as the claim-origin source for the 15-day scorecard, so the quoted counts can be tested without reconstructing them from secondary paraphrase.

The source uses count/effect language that must remain intact: for example, 11 fighter aircraft and helicopters were listed as destroyed or damaged on the ground, alongside separate drone, F-15, P-8, C-17, tanker, heavy-helicopter, HIMARS, Patriot, command-center and hangar claims.
Independent physical reporting establishes that U.S. forces suffered real material damage during the war, so the scorecard cannot be dismissed merely because it came from a belligerent source.
That broader damage record does not independently reconcile the specific 15-day quantities or prove that every listed asset was destroyed rather than damaged.

Atlas therefore treats the exact line items as separate unresolved propositions where the count/effect burden is unmet. Lack of reconciliation is not converted into falsity, and unresolved subclaims do not create a parent Lie finding.

CHAIN-CL-KWI-PATRIOT.public_title: Kuwait airport damage and Patriot-interceptor attribution

public_finding.label: False causal attribution — knowledge not established

CHAIN-CL-KWI-PATRIOT.plain_english_summary: Kuwait International Airport was genuinely damaged during an Iranian missile-and-drone attack. The IRGC/Tasnim attribution that the terminal damage was caused by a U.S. Patriot interceptor is contradicted by Kuwait's attribution of the attack to Iran and the U.S. account that Iranian drones struck the civilian airport. That is enough for a false causal-attribution finding. It is not enough to prove the IRGC spokesman knew the specific terminal impact mechanism was false at statement time; own-force launch knowledge does not automatically equal weapon-impact knowledge amid active interceptions. Atlas therefore publishes the factual falsity but no Lie finding.
how_we_know: Arab News' agency report canonically preserves the IRGC/Tasnim Patriot-interceptor attribution and the U.S. denial in one source record.
Kuwaiti authorities attributed the airport damage and casualties to Iranian attacks; The National independently reports the host-nation attribution.
The physical event is not disputed: the passenger terminal sustained significant material damage and airport operations were disrupted.

The claimant institution plausibly knew what missiles and drones it launched, but the canonical record does not show it possessed discriminating terminal-impact evidence establishing whether a drone, missile, interceptor or debris caused the specific damage when the statement was made.
Because that knowledge component is missing and battlefield misidentification remains credible, the false attribution does not meet the contract's Lie threshold.
open_evidence_gaps: Authenticated weapon-fragment or terminal-impact forensics identifying the exact munition that caused the terminal damage.
Contemporaneous IRGC launch/BDA records showing what the claimant knew about the terminal impact before the Patriot attribution was issued.

CHAIN-CL-200-US-DEAD.public_title: IRGC claim that U.S. military deaths exceeded 200

public_finding.label: False casualty count — no Lie finding

CHAIN-CL-200-US-DEAD.plain_english_summary: The IRGC spokesman's claim that U.S. military fatalities had exceeded 200 is false against the independent casualty record. Reuters reported 18 U.S. service members killed as of July 22, and later AP/Pentagon accounting still did not approach 200. The claim-origin source is now canonical, so the factual proposition is no longer source-blocked. But the current graph does not contain the internal IRGC casualty-estimation basis or evidence showing what Mohebi actually knew when he gave the figure. Atlas therefore publishes FALSE with knowledge insufficient for a Lie finding.
how_we_know: IRNA canonically records the IRGC spokesman's greater-than-200 U.S.-fatality claim.
Reuters' July 22 casualty snapshot reported 18 U.S. service members killed in the war at that point.
Later AP/Pentagon accounting remained nowhere near 200, providing later evidence that adjudicates the earlier count without pretending that later accounting was public at the statement time.
The numerical gap establishes factual falsity, but it does not by itself reveal the internal BDA, assumptions, or casualty-estimation process available to the IRGC spokesman.
Without claimant-access evidence sufficient to distinguish deliberate inflation from catastrophic BDA error, Atlas does not promote the false count to Lie.
open_evidence_gaps: Authenticated IRGC strike/BDA or casualty-estimation records contemporaneous with the July 26 statement.
A separately sourced repetition showing the claimant retained the >200 figure after authoritative contradictory casualty information became available to him.

CHAIN-CL-ERBIL-ALL.public_title: Erbil U.S. infrastructure destruction and operational-effect claim
CHAIN-CL-ERBIL-ALL.plain_english_summary: U.S. positions in the Erbil/Kurdistan theater were repeatedly attacked, and the accepted record preserves real damage as context. The Iranian Army's stronger proposition was that almost all U.S. infrastructure in Erbil had been destroyed and that the relevant presence had effectively lost operational capability. Later independent force-posture reporting shows U.S. troops and military equipment were still being withdrawn from Erbil weeks later. That continuing physical presence and organized drawdown are inconsistent with treating the near-total-destruction/effect language as established. Atlas separates real attack/damage from the overstated scale and functional-effect claims, and does not publish a Lie finding because claimant knowledge is not evidence-complete.
how_we_know: IRNA now supplies the direct source for the Iranian Army's near-total-destruction claim.

Independent AP reporting later confirms that U.S. troops and military equipment remained in Erbil and that an organized drawdown was underway, rather than documenting a near-total physical elimination of the U.S. footprint.
The existence of real attacks or some damage does not prove the 'almost all infrastructure' scale claim.
Conversely, failure of the scale claim does not erase the underlying attack/damage context.

The later force-posture evidence can adjudicate the earlier scale/effect proposition today, but it is not backdated into the claimant's July 26 knowledge. No canonical evidence currently shows what facility-by-facility BDA the Army spokesman possessed.
open_evidence_gaps: Independent facility-by-facility post-strike BDA for the U.S. Erbil footprint as of July 26.
Contemporaneous Iranian Army BDA/command reporting showing the basis for the 'almost all' destruction and operational-effect language.
